title: The Island of the Dolls
summary: For fifty years Don Celestino lived alone on a chinampa in the dark canals of Xochimilco. He hung thousands of dolls from the willows for a little girl he said he found drowned beside his island. Three nights ago he was pulled from the canal himself, at the same spot. No one in Xochimilco can say the girl's name, and the dolls have started whispering again.

characters.name: Chencho the boatman

art.description: thin weathered old trajinero in a sweat-stained straw hat and faded red serape, gray mustache, frightened watery eyes, rosary wrapped around one hand, gripping a long wooden punting pole
idle: standing in his boat leaning on his pole, glancing at the water

dialogue: Quick, señorita, before the lantern dims. I'll say it once.
Three nights ago they found Don Celestino face down in the canal. East bank. The very spot where he always said he found the drowned girl, fifty years back.
His nephew pulled him out. Rufino. He's still up there with candles. I wouldn't be.
A week before, the old man gave me your note. And this key. 'For the señorita who fixes dolls,' he said. Like he knew.
He told me once, one doll in the big willow talks. The one with one eye. He said she listens for the girl.
I took his vegetables to market for forty years. I never once stepped on that island after sundown, and I won't start now.
Take it. The gate. Find your one-eyed doll. And don't look at the water too long.
afterwards: I'll wait here until the lantern burns low. No longer.

characters.name: The One-Eyed Doll

art.description: small old plastic doll in a faded blue dress, gray with grime and cobwebs, hanging by one wrist from rusted wire, one arm missing, matted hair, one blue glass eye open and the other socket empty and dark
idle: hanging by one wrist, head turned to stare at the viewer

dialogue: You came! He said you would. You have mending hands. I can smell the glue.
You think we're decorations? Silly. We're her company.
He brought us so she would play with us at night. With us, and not with the living.
Every night she counts us. When there aren't enough, she whispers. Can you hear her?
Last night she counted one more than before. And he isn't in his house anymore.
His nephew Rufino is in the cabin, there, to the north, sitting with all his candles. He knows how the old man died.
Go on. Ask him. I'll keep watching for you.
afterwards: Shh. She's counting. Don't make me lose my place.

'3 calabazas, 1 muñeca sin brazo.' '1 costal de elote, 4 cabezas.' Squash and corn, traded for dolls.
Your stall is in here too. 'Domingo. La señorita. 2 muñecas quemadas, 5 calabazas.'

characters.name: Rufino

art.description: heavyset Mexican man in his forties in a damp work shirt and jeans, rosary around his neck, red-eyed and unshaven, sitting hunched on an upturned bucket with a yellow flashlight in his lap
idle: sitting hunched on the bucket, flashlight in his lap

dialogue: You're the doll lady. From Chencho's boat. Sit if you want. I'm not going back out there.
Fifty years he hung dolls for her, and nobody in all of Xochimilco can tell me her name.
No grave. Nothing in the parish book. The old women at the market know the story, but not the girl.
Sometimes I think my uncle made her up. A lonely old man, too many years on the water.
But on his last morning he said the sirena had been calling him all night. He said she wouldn't stop.
That evening I found him face down on the east bank. Right where he always said he found her.
His keys weren't on him. They'll be in his fishing net, still snagged in the reeds out there.
Take them if you want them. I'm not going near that water in the dark.
afterwards: I'm not leaving these candles. Not tonight.

characters.name: Don Celestino

art.description: ghost of a small bent old man in a soaked white cotton shirt and trousers, barefoot, sodden straw sombrero, gray skin, duckweed and lake weed on his shoulders, water dripping from hair and fingers, sitting hunched on a low stool wiring a cracked doll head
idle: sitting hunched on a low stool, twisting rusted wire into a cracked doll head

dialogue: Ah, señorita. You came. I knew those mending hands would come.
I found her at dawn, among the lilies, with her little doll floating beside her. I hung the doll in the willow so she would have it.
Then the whispers asked for more. So I gave her company. Fifty years of it. Squash and corn for dolls, dolls from the canals, dolls from your stall.
It was never enough. And she called for me from the water.
The first one, Florinda, is in the shrine past the garden. The shrine key is in the coffee can of eyes, nailed to the willow there.
My scarecrow walks the rows. It doesn't know me anymore. Keep moving. It is slow, but it holds tight.
Here. For the garden gate. (He twists a key out of his wire, and it drips like he does.)
Don't answer if she calls you from the water. I answered too late.
afterwards: I have mending to do. She is waiting.

examine: A rusted coffee can is nailed to the willow at chest height. Its label rotted away long ago.
It's filled to the brim with loose glass doll eyes. Blue, brown, green. Every one of them is turned up, staring at you.
You push your fingers in. They're cold and wet, and they click together like teeth.
Something heavier slides out among them: an orange-painted key with a blue glass eye threaded on its ring.
afterwards: The eyes have settled again. All of them are still looking up at you.

props.name: long stone axolotl trough of stagnant green water
examine: A long stone trough of stagnant green water. Don Celestino kept axolotls here, the little pink creatures of the canals.
Nothing moves in it now. The water is skinned with scum, and the bottom is lost in black silt.
Scratched into the rim with a nail: 'ya no tengo tiempo para nada más que ellas.' I have no time anymore for anything but them.

parts.art: old gray porcelain doll sitting upright, rotted lace dress, long crack across her forehead, glass eyes staring, front view

examine: Florinda sits in the black water, her lace gone to rot. The crack across her forehead is wide enough to fit two fingers.
Inside her porcelain head is a folded paper, dry somehow. The old man's shaking hand:
'I heard her that evening. A little girl crying for help in the canal.'
'I told myself it was the sirena singing. I barred my door and I sang until it stopped.'
'In the morning I found her in the lilies. Every doll since is my apology. She cannot be left alone.'
It was never about the doll. Under Florinda, the water in the tub is rising. It spills over the rim and does not stop.

Under it, a faded photograph: Don Celestino as a young man, standing by the canal, holding a porcelain doll in both hands.
It's Florinda. His face is pale, and he is not smiling.
On the back, in pencil: 'el primer día.' The first day.
Across the hut, in the candlelight, something sits in a tin washtub, waiting.
afterwards: The young man in the photo holds the doll away from his body, as if she might bite.

characters.name: La Niña del Teshuilo

art.description: barefoot drowned girl about eight, soaked and dripping, little dress gray-green with canal mud and duckweed, long black hair like lake weed, pale gray skin crazed with porcelain cracks stitched with rusted wire, dead water lilies on her shoulders, one arm hanging at a wrong doll-like angle

characters.scream: A little girl's scream gargled through a throat full of water, bubbling and choking. Under it, hundreds of doll voice boxes cry 'mamá' at once, rising into a shriek.
characters.jumpscare: Her cracked porcelain face fills the screen. Two glass doll eyes roll loose in her sockets and snap forward to stare. Her jaw unhinges far too wide, like a broken doll's, and black canal water and duckweed pour out over her chin. Rusted wire stitches split open across her cheeks.

intro.art: A trajinera with a faded painted name arch glides down a black Xochimilco canal at night. A single kerosene lantern hangs on its prow, and mist lies on the water. Ahead, the low island rises, its ahuejote willows silhouetted against a green-tinged moon. Hundreds of dolls hang from every branch, pale faces and dangling limbs catching the lantern light.
text: You mend broken dolls at a market stall in Mexico City. For twenty years an old man from the canals of Xochimilco came on Sundays. He bought the dolls you couldn't save, armless, headless, burned, and he paid in squash and corn.

Three nights ago, Don Celestino was pulled from the canal beside his island, at the spot where, he always said, he once found a little girl drowned. For fifty years he hung dolls in the willows for her. Thousands of them.
This morning a boatman brought you a note in the old man's shaking hand: 'Señorita, if the water takes me, come for the first one. She cannot be left alone. Come at night. She only talks at night.'
The boatman would only bring you after dark. Now his trajinera knocks against the island landing, and in the trees above you a thousand dolls turn slowly in a wind you cannot feel.
